identity.spiritualSignificanceShort: Shirdi Sai Baba Temple, formally the Shri Saibaba Samadhi Mandir, houses the marble memorial of Sai Baba of Shirdi (c. 1838 – 15 October 1918), a spiritual teacher venerated by both Hindu and Muslim devotees who, when asked about his own religious identity, declined to align himself exclusively with either tradition. It is not a temple to a classical Hindu deity avatar but a samadhi shrine to a revered saint/guru figure, and it is among the highest-footfall pilgrimage sites in India.

narrative.summaryIntro:
Shirdi Sai Baba Temple is a pilgrimage complex in the town of Shirdi, in Maharashtra's Ahilyanagar (historically Ahmednagar) district, built around the samadhi (memorial) of Sai Baba of Shirdi. Sai Baba was a spiritual teacher who lived in the village for most of his life until his death in 1918 and was revered by both Hindu and Muslim followers; he consistently declined to identify himself exclusively with either religion. Because he is honoured as a saint and guru rather than as an avatar of a classical deity, the temple sits outside the usual Shaiva, Vaishnava or Shakta classifications.

The complex is administered by the Shree Saibaba Sansthan Trust and, alongside the Samadhi Mandir, includes several other sites tied to Baba's life: Dwarkamai, the mosque where he lived for over sixty years; Chavadi, his alternate sleeping quarters; Gurusthan, the site under a neem tree where he was first seen in the village; and Lendi Baug, a garden he tended. The temple draws tens of thousands of pilgrims daily and is administered as an attached office of the Government of Maharashtra's Law and Judiciary Department.
narrative.documentedHistory:
Sai Baba of Shirdi (c. 1838 – 15 October 1918) arrived in the village of Shirdi around the age of sixteen and settled there permanently from about 1858. He first practiced austerities beneath a neem tree at a spot now known as Gurusthan, before villagers persuaded him to take up residence in a dilapidated mosque that he renamed Dwarkamai, where he maintained a continuously burning sacred fire and lived mainly on alms for the rest of his life. He also tended a garden known as Lendi Baug. His teaching emphasised self-realisation and a moral code of love, forgiveness, charity, contentment and devotion to God, and he rejected discrimination by caste or religion; when devotees pressed him on his own religious affiliation he refused to identify himself to the exclusion of either Hinduism or Islam, recommending Hindu scriptures to Hindu visitors and the Qur'an to Muslim ones.

Sai Baba died on 15 October 1918, coinciding with Vijayadashami. His remains were interred at Buti Wada, a building begun by the Nagpur devotee Shreemant Gopalrao Buti as a residential mansion for Baba, which became the core of the present Samadhi Mandir. According to the Ahilyanagar district administration, the temple complex's principal sites — the Samadhi Mandir, Dwarkamai, Gurusthan and the nearby Khandoba and Mhasoba temples — lie within about a kilometre of one another and can be covered on foot. Baba's samadhi in the Mandir is built of white marble.

The temple is administered by the Shree Saibaba Sansthan Trust, which, per the temple's Wikipedia article, also runs associated charitable hospitals, educational institutions and social-welfare services. The Government of Maharashtra's Law and Judiciary Department lists 'Shri Saibaba Temple, Shirdi' among its attached offices, confirming the trust's official website, a contact telephone number, and the Shirdi address with postal code 423109. The trust's own website warns devotees to rely only on its two official web addresses (sai.org.in and online.sai.org.in) for bookings and donations, citing fraudulent look-alike sites.
narrative.architectureStyle: Composite pilgrimage complex built up through the 20th century around Buti Wada; no single classical temple style documented in sources reviewed

editorial.verificationNotes: Core identity, governance and contact details are corroborated across the temple's own trust website, its contact page, and a Maharashtra government department listing. Darshan opening time and the daily aarti schedule come from the trust's home page, which does not state a closing time, a dress code, an entry-fee structure, or specific transit distances in kilometres — none of these are recorded here. History and site descriptions beyond governance lean on Wikipedia and the district tourism page; no academic or inscriptional source was located for this temple.

visitingInfo.officialContactNote: Confirm same-day darshan and aarti timings with the trust's main office at +91 2423 258500, or the helpline numbers +91 7588375204 / 7588371245 / 7588373189 / 7588374469, before travelling. The trust warns devotees to use only sai.org.in and online.sai.org.in for bookings and donations, citing fraudulent websites, phone numbers and map listings using its name.
